stories.headline: Fred VanVleet's 'fresh slate' is driving Houston's early season success
stories.summary: A healthy Fred VanVleet is commanding the surging Rockets after an ACL injury derailed his 2025-26 season. Here's why he's so important.
stories.body:
FRED VANVLEET BOILED inside watching the Houston Rockets "floating," he'd later say, as the Utah Jazz transformed a 12-point deficit into a 10-point lead over a span of 7 minutes, 39 seconds of a game he knew "was there for the taking."

"He was pissed off," Rockets coach Ime Udoka said, "and kind of went off on everybody."

VanVleet also unleashed that fury on the Jazz, who eventually fell 125-118 on Nov. 13 in an NBA Cup matchup, as VanVleet racked up 10 of his 17 points in the third quarter, catalyzing a 15-2 Rockets run heading into the final period.

Alperen Sengun jokingly revealed a new nickname for the point guard after the game: "Admiral."

VanVleet, 32, is navigating his NBA career now with more purpose, after acknowledging he had taken it for granted. It's a realization VanVleet came to while sitting out a 2025-26 campaign that teemed with expectations after Kevin Durant's arrival. The point guard sustained a torn ACL at a workout in the Bahamas before training camp, leaving the Rockets without a veteran floor leader and bound for a second straight first-round postseason exit.

But the undersized, self-made veteran is steering the ship again in Houston. VanVleet is transforming the Rockets into contenders in the Western Conference, sitting at 12-4 and one game out of the 1-seed.

The Rockets currently rank 10th in assist-to-turnover ratio and 14th in turnover percentage, after finishing 27th in both of those categories last season. VanVleet ranks fifth in the NBA in assist-to-turnover ratio (5.07) among players logging at least 25 minutes per game.

He has also improved Houston's spacing, having taken 66% of his shots from 3-point range, good for ninth among players to attempt 100 shots or more. He's also knocking down those long balls, connecting on 39.8% from range, which would register as the second-best 3-point percentage of his career.

Most of all, VanVleet provides the calming steady hand that Houston missed in his absence last season. The Rockets finished 22-23 last season in clutch time -- defined by any game separated by five points or fewer in the final five minutes of the fourth quarter or overtime -- with VanVleet watching from the bench.

"We obviously missed his end-of-game stuff last season, but just his calming presence on the court, getting guys set in their spots [is what VanVleet provides]," Udoka told ESPN. "He always takes what the game gives him. So, he's picking the spots as far as scoring and getting guys involved. Some of our end-game situations last year were due to a lack of I would say poise at the end from a veteran leader."

VANVLEET POINTS OUT he was having "one of my best summers" when word came down the Rockets were trading for Durant in June.

For VanVleet, adding Durant "symbolized at that moment that, 'OK, we're competing for a championship this year.' And that was the part that was like, 'All right, boom, I've got to get my mind ready and get right to compete for a chip.'"

VanVleet had already taken care of the physical part of preparation. Then in late July, he boarded a near 12-hour flight to Istanbul, where he spent a week working with Sengun to optimize pick-and-roll actions and angles on screens. VanVleet and Sengun also participated in 3-on-3 and 5-on-5 runs against members of the Turkish national team.

By the time the Rockets convened in the Bahamas ahead of training camp, the first day the entire team was together in the gym, VanVleet wanted to impart some wisdom on playing alongside a generational superstar.

VanVleet was part of the 2019 Toronto Raptors squad that defeated Durant's Golden State Warriors in six games after a midseason trade with the San Antonio Spurs sent Kawhi Leonard to Toronto.

"I was letting everybody know because I went through it with Kawhi [Leonard]," VanVleet said. "Nothing changes just because we added KD. We've still got to be us."

Naturally, VanVleet would demonstrate on the court in an open gym run with his teammates. "So, I'm having a day," he said. "I'm balling."

Then, just as quickly, something in his right leg popped.

"You could feel the air come out of the gym," VanVleet said. "Then, we did little tests and s--- like that. I didn't think it was that bad. I thought maybe I'd be out a couple weeks, maybe miss the preseason.

"But ultimately, when we got the MRI, that's when it was real."

VanVleet underwent ACL surgery that September and vowed to return to the team later that season, not because he believed he'd recover quickly to join them on the court, "but just to keep the guys locked in," VanVleet explained. "Just because I went down don't mean to give up the f---ing season."

VanVleet wouldn't let them, anyway. A couple of weeks after the surgery, his phone started to buzz with texts from teammates that he acknowledges kept him focused throughout the rehab process.

"Yo, we need you around," one text read.

Another said: "We just need you here. We need your voice."

VanVleet couldn't walk for five weeks after the surgery and said he had to learn to run and jump again.

"I'm appreciative now of every second of what it means to be in the NBA," he said. "You can lose sight of that. It's just natural as a human. We just take advantage. You take for granted your health until you wake up and you've got the flu. Everybody walking around is taking for granted walking."

VanVleet would spend all of last season at most of the team's meetings, practices and games -- both home and away -- working with some of younger players such as Amen Thompson and Reed Sheppard on pick-and-roll reads as the Rockets tried to replace their veteran point guard with inexperienced ball handlers.

Thompson had spent his first two seasons locked mainly into the dunker spot, and the coaching staff pushed him into learning a totally new position so he could serve as VanVleet's primary replacement. Sheppard was coming off a rookie season in which he started only three games and played primarily off the ball. Durant, Sengun, Jabari Smith Jr. and Tari Eason would all take turns throughout the season initiating the offense. But none of them could match VanVleet's reliability, especially late in games.

Game 3 of Houston's opening-round loss to the Los Angeles Lakers showed just how much.

With Durant out because of a sore left ankle, the Rockets led by six points with 30 seconds remaining, on the verge of winning their first game of the series. Then, things went haywire for an inexperienced squad missing their floor leader.

First, Houston fouled on a 3-point attempt with 25 seconds left in regulation after a turnover, and the Lakers knocked down all three free throws to pull to within three points.

Then, LeBron James picked Sheppard clean for a steal and hit a 3-pointer to tie the score at 101 with 13 seconds left.

Those "horrendous mistakes," as Udoka described them that night, caused Houston to fall 112-108 in overtime. The Rockets eventually lost the series 4-2.

"He would tell me [during that time] to just take it a day at a time," Thompson told ESPN about VanVleet. "It was a new thing. Going from playing damn near power forward to point guard it's different. He knows there's a lot that comes with that. That first year for point guards is hard. So, he was always keeping me locked in. He was genuinely great."

Still, all the time spent off the floor playing pseudo-coach changed how VanVleet viewed his career.

"Because of my story and where I come from, I always felt like I had good perspective," VanVleet said. "I felt like I was always very appreciative of the moment and grateful. But you don't really have a real understanding of that until it's taken away from you. So, to not be able to play, to not be active, to sit out a full year, it gives you an appreciation for the small s---. I've had a hell of a career so far and now it's like, 'OK, you get another chance to have a fresh slate.'"

ON A COOL, damp Tuesday at Memorial Hermann, the Rockets' training center, Udoka cracked a smile, pondering the notion of VanVleet's ability to hold his coaching staff just as accountable as his teammates.

"He's the most vocal," Udoka said. "He's got the IQ, experience, all those things. We can move him all around. For instance, put him on guards one night. Put him on Draymond Green another night, different things like that and he recognizes everything. He has a really good feel for what to get us into to get guys shots, and a feel for who needs to get involved, who to keep hot."

Udoka says he considers VanVleet an extension of the coaching staff, holding everyone on staff accountable.

VanVleet's return has eased the ballhandling burden of both Thompson and Durant, which has played a role in reducing turnovers. Durant finished last season with the 10th-most turnovers (3.2 per game) in the NBA, and now his touches per game (50.3) are his fewest in a season since player tracking began in 2013. Durant's 3.1-second average touch length ranks as his lowest in a season since 2016-17 after finishing 2025-26 with the highest touch length (3.8 seconds) of his career.

Thompson, meanwhile, has brought the ball up the court this season for an average of 20.2 possessions, down from 31.4 last season, and his average touch length has fallen from 3.8 seconds last season to 3.1.

"It's just control," Smith said. "It's ball security, just knowing what we're going to get to when he's on the floor. The main thing late in the games is getting up shots and not turning the ball over. He adds that ball security and knows how to slow down the game, knowing what we're going to get to, what set we're going to run and what matchup we like."

The Rockets have faced four of the top eight teams in the West, winning three of those matchups, including victories over the Spurs, Denver Nuggets and Oklahoma City Thunder. Though Houston's 3-3 record in clutch time isn't much better than last season's mark (22-23), the team has cut turnovers in clutch time in half from 1.6 to 0.8 -- a direct result of VanVleet's steady hand in crucial moments.

The veteran has dished 71 assists with 14 turnovers so far.

VanVleet will become an unrestricted free agent at the end of the season. But he isn't approaching what could be his final season in Houston with a chip on his shoulder. Throughout the early portion of the schedule, he has sat out of the second night of back-to-backs but hopes to ramp up his workload to play every night as the season progresses.

"I believe in betting on yourself, but I never really played for myself," VanVleet said. "I believe the better the team does, it's a reflection on me. I made a s--- ton of money based on being good to the game, being a good teammate and playing the right way. So, I'm not going to change that now."

VanVleet demonstrated as much with his third-quarter tongue lashing on the Rockets' bench against the Jazz on Nov. 13, the same night Sengun became the third player in Rockets history to tally 40 points, 10 rebounds and 5 assists on 70% shooting, joining the company of Yao Ming (2004) and Hakeem Olajuwon (1994). VanVleet has thrived with on-ball screens this season, ranking seventh in points per direct pick among ball handlers to run 100-plus plays. He also has been an extremely effective partner working with Sengun in inverted pick-and-rolls.

"He comes out there, wakes everybody up, plays his ass off, and helps everybody," Sengun said.

ESPN Research contributed to this story.

stories.headline: As Nike replaces Adidas, is UEFA Champions League star ball on its way out?
stories.summary: Nike will replace Adidas as supplier of UEFA Champions League match balls from next season. Will the famous 'star ball' design soon be no more?
stories.body:
Editor's note: This article was first published on Aug. 26, 2026 and has been updated

The UEFA Champions League and UEFA Women's Champions League match balls will boast a brand new look starting next season after UEFA confirmed on Monday that Nike will be taking over from long-standing provider Adidas as the official supplier for the 2027-28 campaign onwards.

Nike will take the reins for the 2027-28 campaign onward after agreeing a deal to supply the official match balls for all three UEFA club competitions from 2027 to 2031 -- the Champions League, the Europa League and the Conference League. According to The Guardian, that deal is worth around $45 million a year, double the value of the final contract with Adidas.

- Man United, Pochettino's to-do list based on what's gone wrong

- Meet Como's Paz, the heir to Messi's Argentina No. 10 shirt

- Champions League talking points: Are Como the real deal?

With Adidas having supplied the official Champions League match ball since 2001, the "star ball" design has become an emblem of the competition. However, the last we see of the iconic pattern might be in the 2026-27 final.

That's because, as things stand, there are no specific details available as to the designs that Nike has in store. In a statement on Monday, UEFA would only say: "Further details on the match ball designs will be revealed in due course." It is also unclear -- and highly unlikely -- that the American sportswear giant will continue with the star theme popularised by Adidas over the past 25 years, as the German powerhouse reportedly hold the rights to the star ball design.

Nike's designs are therefore likely to be fresh and distinct with the intent of drawing a line under Adidas' tenure as UEFA match ball suppliers while also launching their own, modernised visual identity.

Back in August, Adidas unveiled what will be their final iteration of the "star ball," the preliminary eye-catching colourway of which is currently being used throughout the group phase of the 2026-27 Champions League.

The men's version of the 2026-27 Champions League ball is plastered in a neon-spattered livery that, according to Adidas, has been inspired by players creating colourful moments of magic and personal expression while plugging away at training on cold, foggy training pitches during their quest to attain Champions League greatness.

The design for the women's match ball is a little less abstract. The golden-orange pattern takes its inspiration from the aura of the ring of 11 stars that make up the UWCL emblem, with flashes of metallic purple and silver then adding a dash of visual contrast to the mix.

Both balls are based on the template that Adidas have used for their Champions League match balls since the introduction of the "Finale 1" ball for the 2001-02 season. Since then, over 50 iterations of the UCL star ball have been deployed in the competition -- and that's not including the various hi-vis yellow variants that have been used in winter months over the years.

stories.headline: NHL Power Rankings: Updated poll, plus fantasy hockey add/drops for all 32 teams
stories.summary: The Hurricanes remain atop the list, while the Senators made a big leap.
stories.body:
The NHL has passed the mathematical quarter mark of the 2026-27 season (although the spiritual quarter mark is American Thanksgiving next week Thursday).

Nevertheless, it's time for another set of Power Rankings, as voted on by a panel of ESPN puckheads.

This week, it's time for another fantasy hockey takeover! Sean Allen (Eastern Conference) and Victoria Matiash (West) identify one player to add or drop from all 32 teams.

And a reminder: It's not too late to play ESPN fantasy hockey, with new leagues starting every Monday.

How we rank: A panel of ESPN hockey commentators, analysts, reporters and editors sends a 1-32 poll based on the games through Wednesday. Those ballots are combined to come up with the rankings you see below.

Note: Previous ranking for each team refers to the previous edition, published Nov. 13. Points percentages through the games of Nov. 19.

1. Carolina Hurricanes
Previous ranking: 1

Points percentage: 79.55%

Drop Brandon Bussi, G (0.35 fantasy points per game, 52.6% rostered): Bussi has lost the crease battle. Pyotr Kochetkov has taken most of Carolina's starts and posted far better numbers, while Bussi's save percentage sits well below .900. A backup on a great team can still steal wins, but not often enough to hold a roster spot in most leagues.

Next seven days: vs. EDM (Nov. 21), @ NYR (Nov. 22), @ TB (Nov. 25)

2. Edmonton Oilers
Previous ranking: 4

Points percentage: 77.08%

Add Devon Levi, G (3.82 FPPG, 43.6% available): Embracing his inner Maximus Decimus Meridius, with the online support of cinematic gladiator Russell Crowe, Levi is 4-0-0 with a .947 SV%, 1.25 GAA since returning from injury. The young goalie has swagger, the Oilers are playing solid defense, and Connor McDavid & Co. can still always score their way out of other problems any day of the week. Pick him up.

Next seven days: @ CAR (Nov. 21), @ STL (Nov. 22), vs. VGK (Nov. 24)

3. Minnesota Wild
Previous ranking: 2

Points percentage: 79.17%

Add Filip Gustavsson, G (N/A FPPG, 49.9% available): The veteran netminder's return is imminent. Which is helpful, since Jesper Wallstedt is on pace to start 73 games this regular season. Not an ideal tempo for a team gunning to win the Cup in a few months. While Gustavsson won't compete as much as the early Vezina Trophy favorite, he'll see enough action to satisfy managers in deeper fantasy leagues.

Next seven days: @ VAN (Nov. 21), @ SJ (Nov. 23), vs. UTA (Nov. 25)

4. Tampa Bay Lightning
Previous ranking: 5

Points percentage: 72.73%

Add Anthony Cirelli, C (1.66 FPPG, 79.0% available): Cirelli has seen time alongside Nikita Kucherov and Brandon Hagel, and he has been producing at a steady clip. His track record says this is close to who he is. At 21% rostered, he's a bargain.

Next seven days: vs. BUF (Nov. 22), vs. CAR (Nov. 25)

5. New Jersey Devils
Previous ranking: 6

Points percentage: 68.18%

Add Connor Brown, RW (1.71 FPPG, 97.0% available): Brown has landed a regular spot on New Jersey's power play and has been cashing in. Fair warning: he's scoring more than his chances suggest, so the pace will slow. With Anthony Mantha out until at least mid-December, ride the role while it lasts.

Next seven days: @ STL (Nov. 21), vs. CBJ (Nov. 23), @ CBJ (Nov. 25)

6. Ottawa Senators
Previous ranking: 12

Points percentage: 67.39%

Drop Dylan Cozens, C/RW (1.47 FPPG, 73.6% rostered): Cozens has lost ground on Ottawa's power play, with his time on the man advantage down by about a minute a night lately. Without that, his fantasy value leans mostly on hits. His hits still help in leagues that count them, but without the power-play time, there isn't enough scoring to go with them.

Next seven days: vs. LA (Nov. 21), vs. CGY (Nov. 23), @ FLA (Nov. 25)

7. Boston Bruins
Previous ranking: 3

Points percentage: 65.91%

Add Pavel Zacha, C (1.59 FPPG, 50.4% available): Zacha's low roster rate is a hangover from a slow start, when he managed one point in his first five games. He has been producing steadily since, back alongside David Pastrnak, the same partnership that paid off last season, with more than four minutes of power-play time a night. Boston has outscored opponents at 5-on-5 when that line is out, so this one is real.

Next seven days: vs. WSH (Nov. 21), vs. WPG (Nov. 25)

8. Montreal Canadiens
Previous ranking: 8

Points percentage: 69.57%

Drop Noah Dobson, D (1.45 FPPG, 87.7% rostered): Dobson's problem is role. He's stuck on Montreal's second power-play unit, and a defender without top-unit time needs peripherals to matter. His hits and blocks are middling at best. In standard leagues, the spot is better used elsewhere.

Next seven days: vs. PHI (Nov. 21), vs. LA (Nov. 23), @ COL (Nov. 25)

9. Vegas Golden Knights
Previous ranking: 7

Points percentage: 64.58%

Drop Shea Theodore, D (1.32 FPPG, 54.6% rostered): No member of Vegas' blue line is making much productive noise this fall, including the 31-yer-old puck-moving defenseman. It doesn't help that coach Ryan Craig is rolling out a top power play consisting of five forwards, a group that's getting the job done rather effectively.

Next seven days: @ WPG (Nov. 21), @ EDM (Nov. 24)

10. Dallas Stars
Previous ranking: 10

Points percentage: 68.18%

Add Esa Lindell, D (1.46 FPPG, 65.8% available): The longtime Star is averaging 0.33 points/game since his third full year in 2018-19. While hardly a jaw-dropping rate, one that suggests the 32-year-old defender is ready to mildly erupt after pitching in just one point in 16 games this fall. Toss in his enduringly dependable number of blocked shots, and Lindell could prove once again valuable in deeper fantasy leagues very soon.

Next seven days: vs. PIT (Nov. 22), vs. NSH (Nov. 25)

11. Colorado Avalanche
Previous ranking: 9

Points percentage: 63.04%

Drop Scott Wedgewood, G (-1.71 FPPG, 58.9% rostered): Heading into Thursday's contests against the Ducks, Wedgewood's thriving 2025-26 campaign feels like an eon ago now. If the singular win, .863 SV% and 3.99 GAA doesn't serve as perturbing, then the 6.95 GSAx should. Especially since Mackenzie Blackwood is performing well. Time to comb the wire for other goaltending options.

Next seven days: vs. MTL (Nov. 25)

12. New York Rangers
Previous ranking: 18

Points percentage: 61.36%

Drop J.T. Miller, C/LW (1.59 FPPG, 79.3% rostered): Some of Miller's slow start is bad luck, but not all of it. His power-play time has slipped lately, and his line has been outscored at 5-on-5. At nearly 80% rostered, his roster rate is living off reputation more than production.

Next seven days: vs. CAR (Nov. 22), @ BUF (Nov. 25)

13. Nashville Predators
Previous ranking: 11

Points percentage: 61.36%

Drop Brady Skjei, D (1.1 FPPG, 34.3% rostered): The well-rounded defender in real life doesn't shoot, score, hit or block enough shots to justify investment in just about any form of NHL fantasy competition. Moreso, there's a good gaggle of widely available blueliners who are easily banging out more than 1.1 fantasy points per outing.

Next seven days: vs. PIT (Nov. 21), @ DAL (Nov. 25)

14. Florida Panthers
Previous ranking: 14

Points percentage: 58.7%

Drop Sam Bennett, C (1.44 FPPG, 72.0% rostered): Bennett's power-play time has been cut roughly in half lately, and without it, his fantasy line leans on hits. He's a better real-life player than fantasy starter, and the roster spot can do more elsewhere.

Next seven days: vs. BUF (Nov. 21), vs. OTT (Nov. 25)

15. New York Islanders
Previous ranking: 20

Points percentage: 59.52%

Add Brayden Schenn, C/LW (1.79 FPPG, 68.4% available): Schenn has been one of the Islanders' most productive forwards lately, and his line has controlled the scoreboard at 5-on-5. The bonus is the physical play: more than two hits a night gives him a floor in leagues that count them.

Next seven days: @ DET (Nov. 21), vs. TOR (Nov. 23), vs. STL (Nov. 25)

16. Utah Mammoth
Previous ranking: 15

Points percentage: 54.35%

Drop Karel Vejmelka, G (-0.4 FPPG, 85.7% rostered): Head coach Andre Tourigny: "He has a job to do. He needs to do it. Now more than ever ... we need him big time." In fact, Vejmelka hasn't been holding up his part of the bargain these first few weeks, sporting a career-worst .872 SV% and, more worrisome, a minus-7.89 GSAx. Until (if/when) the 30-year-old figures it out, he's doing more fantasy damage than good.

Next seven days: vs. ANA (Nov. 21), @ WPG (Nov. 23), @ MIN (Nov. 25)

17. Washington Capitals
Previous ranking: 13

Points percentage: 50%

Drop Alex Ovechkin, LW/RW (0.68 FPPG, 69.5% rostered): This one stings. Ovechkin is still getting good looks and has scored far fewer goals than his chances deserve. But even with normal luck, the 41-year-old projects as a depth winger at about 13 minutes per game. With retirement already announced, there's no keeper case either. Enjoy the farewell tour as a fan, not a manager.

Next seven days: @ BOS (Nov. 21), vs. PHI (Nov. 25)

18. Anaheim Ducks
Previous ranking: 16

Points percentage: 50%

Add Judd Caulfield, RW (1.53 FPPG, 96.6% available): Who? The newest member of the Ducks' top line and power play, that's who. Units that also include the league's co-leader in goals, Cutter Gauthier. Unlike Gauthier, Beckett Sennecke, Leo Carlsson and other heavy-fantasy-hitters in Anaheim, Caulfield is both useful -- at least right now in deeper leagues -- and widely available.

Next seven days: @ UTA (Nov. 21), @ SEA (Nov. 23), vs. SJ (Nov. 25)

19. St. Louis Blues
Previous ranking: 21

Points percentage: 54.55%

Drop Colton Parayko, D (1.54 FPPG, 60.2% rostered): The second-pair defender isn't scoring, shooting, hitting or blocking enough shots to merit rostering in conventional ESPN Fantasy leagues. Drop Parayko for fellow blueliner Philip Broberg, who's skating on the Blues' No. 1 power play and has 14 points to show for 21 games to date.

Next seven days: vs. NJ (Nov. 21), vs. EDM (Nov. 22), @ NYI (Nov. 25)

20. Winnipeg Jets
Previous ranking: 22

Points percentage: 54.35%

Add Gabriel Vilardi, RW (1.47 FPPG, 40.6% available): Boosted (once more) to the Jets' top line and power play, Vilardi has two goals and six assists on 20 shots in his past seven contests. The imposing, minute-munching winger is one reason Winnipeg is winning more games than not these days.

Next seven days: vs. VGK (Nov. 21), vs. UTA (Nov. 23), @ BOS (Nov. 25)

21. Seattle Kraken
Previous ranking: 17

Points percentage: 55.26%

Drop Vince Dunn, D (1.81 FPPG, 76.3% rostered): There just isn't enough meat on the fantasy bone to justify rostering Dunn in all but the most profound of deeper fantasy leagues. For one, it's difficult to get too excited about a blueliner's role on a top power play when they have only two assists with the extra skater to show for their most recent 14 games.

Next seven days: @ SJ (Nov. 21), vs. ANA (Nov. 23), vs. CHI (Nov. 25)

22. Buffalo Sabres
Previous ranking: 19

Points percentage: 50%

Add Zach Benson, LW (1.58 FPPG, 69.7% available): Benson has scored far less often than his chances deserve, and that's the opening. He's skating more than 20 minutes a night with heavy power-play time, and his assists have kept him useful while the goals lag. The role is right, and the scoring should catch up.

Next seven days: @ FLA (Nov. 21), @ TB (Nov. 22), vs. NYR (Nov. 25)

23. Calgary Flames
Previous ranking: 25

Points percentage: 45.65%

Add Dustin Wolf, G (-0.1 FPPG, 75.2% available): If only as a temp in net for the next couple of weeks. After an ugly October, Wolf is on the upswing with a 4-1-1 record, .919 SV% and 2.18 GAA heading into Thursday's tilt with the Wild. Backstopping a Flames squad that's gutting out some impressive wins, he merits tossing out against several opponents in the coming days, such as the Blackhawks, Penguins, Rangers, Red Wings and Sabres.

Next seven days: vs. CHI (Nov. 21), @ OTT (Nov. 23), @ PIT (Nov. 25)

24. San Jose Sharks
Previous ranking: 26

Points percentage: 45.83%

Drop Darnell Nurse, D (1.36 FPPG, 61.0% rostered): Surprisingly to most, he was much more valuable as a fantasy performer back in Edmonton. As it stands, Nurse's moderate total of hits plus blocked shots doesn't come anywhere near making up for his measly three points through 23 contests.

Next seven days: vs. SEA (Nov. 21), vs. MIN (Nov. 23), @ ANA (Nov. 25)

25. Detroit Red Wings
Previous ranking: 24

Points percentage: 43.18%

Add Viktor Arvidsson, RW (1.78 FPPG, 53.4% available): Arvidsson has cooled off, but the chances haven't. He's getting quality looks and a big share of Detroit's power-play time. If someone in your league cut him during the dip, he's worth grabbing before the finish catches up.

Next seven days: vs. NYI (Nov. 21), vs. VAN (Nov. 25)

26. Pittsburgh Penguins
Previous ranking: 28

Points percentage: 38.1%

Add Tommy Novak, C/LW (1.71 FPPG, 82.8% available): Novak keeps finding a way. He's logging nearly three minutes of power-play time a night lately, and with Bryan Rust out until at least early December, Pittsburgh needs his scoring. He brings almost nothing in hits or blocks, so his value rides on points, and in deeper leagues, that's enough.

Next seven days: @ NSH (Nov. 21), @ DAL (Nov. 22), vs. CGY (Nov. 25)

27. Toronto Maple Leafs
Previous ranking: 23

Points percentage: 39.58%

Drop John Tavares, C (1.63 FPPG, 76.6% rostered): Toronto has struggled, and Tavares is caught in it. The Leafs have been badly outscored at 5-on-5 with him on the ice. The 36-year-old still has a power-play role, but that isn't enough to justify a roster spot in standard leagues.

Next seven days: vs. CBJ (Nov. 21), @ NYI (Nov. 23)

28. Philadelphia Flyers
Previous ranking: 30

Points percentage: 44%

Add Jamie Drysdale, D (1.69 FPPG, 77.4% available): Drysdale is getting the role fantasy managers have long waited for. He's seeing more than 23 minutes a night, and Philadelphia leans on him for the bulk of its power-play time. He won't shoot much, but the assists and minutes make him a solid depth defender.

Next seven days: @ MTL (Nov. 21), @ WSH (Nov. 25)

29. Los Angeles Kings
Previous ranking: 29

Points percentage: 40%

Add Kevin Fiala, LW (0.7 FPPG, 47.3% available): Give it a minute. After suffering a devastating broken leg at last winter's Olympics, the winger will understandably need a bit of time to get back up to speed. Skating in L.A.'s top six and on the No. 1 power play, it shouldn't take too long. Since 2020-21, Fiala has produced at a 0.85 point/game pace.

Next seven days: @ OTT (Nov. 21), @ MTL (Nov. 23)

30. Columbus Blue Jackets
Previous ranking: 27

Points percentage: 40%

Add Kent Johnson, LW/RW (2.04 FPPG, 52.0% available): Johnson has been the bright spot in a rough Columbus season, producing at a near top-line fantasy rate with a steady power-play role. He's skating more than 18 minutes a night, and the opportunity isn't going anywhere. On a thin roster, he's one of the few Blue Jackets you can trust for points.

Next seven days: @ TOR (Nov. 21), @ NJ (Nov. 23), vs. NJ (Nov. 25)

31. Chicago Blackhawks
Previous ranking: 31

Points percentage: 31.82%

Add Frank Nazar, C (1.82 FPPG, 84.8% available): There's no ignoring the seven goals, including three with the extra skater, in only six games. Toss in the shots, short-handed point, hits etc., and it works out to a productive run from the third-year skater. Plus, the Blackhawks will need even more from the Nazar if Connor Bedard is to miss significant time.

Next seven days: @ CGY (Nov. 21), @ VAN (Nov. 22), @ SEA (Nov. 25)

32. Vancouver Canucks
Previous ranking: 32

Points percentage: 22.92%

Add Brock Boeser, RW (2.14 FPPG, 25.4% available): While we all oooh and ahhh over the flashy figures put up by other stars around the league, Boeser is going about his quiet business of essentially kicking in a point, at minimum, every game. The Canucks' winger has failed to produce a goal or assist only twice since Oct. 11.

Next seven days: vs. MIN (Nov. 21), vs. CHI (Nov. 22), @ DET (Nov. 25)

stories.headline: F1 bosses confirm 'agreement' on V8 engine return deal
stories.summary: McLaren CEO Zak Brown has confirmed that an "agreement in principle" exists for Formula 1 to switch to V8 engines, with the final details being worked on ahead of a proposed introduction in 2030.
stories.body:
McLaren CEO Zak Brown has confirmed that an "agreement in principle" exists for Formula 1 to switch to V8 engines, with the final details being worked on ahead of a proposed introduction in 2030.

Brown's comments follow a post on social media by FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem earlier this week that stated: "You spoke, we listened. V8s coming soon."

Ben Sulayem's post coincided with what appeared to be an official announcement on the FIA's own social media channels, only for those details to be quickly deleted.

Brown said on Thursday at the Las Vegas Grand Prix that there were still elements to be decided, but that the overarching agreement on V8 engines was in place.

"There's an agreement in principle," he said. "I think everyone is very, very excited. I think now it's about kind of dotting the i's and crossing the t's."

The plan to introduce the new engine formula was discussed during a meeting of F1, the FIA, teams and power unit manufacturers on Tuesday in London.

Fast-tracking the change for 2030 would see the current engine regulation cycle, which was introduced at the start of this year, cut short by one year.

The existing regulations, which feature 1.6-litre V6 turbo-hybrids, have been criticised by drivers for being overcomplicated, with four-time champion Max Verstappen labelling the current power units "anti-racing" at the start of the year.

The plan discussed on Tuesday is for F1 to introduce 2.1-litre turbocharged V8s with a less powerful hybrid element than the current power units.

- Antonelli handed grid penalty for Las Vegas GP; Russell sets pace in FP2

- Max Verstappen on F1 retirement, Le Mans and learning to lose: 'Stress a bit less'

- FIA to introduce full-time stewards to address worries over decision-making

The next step is for the final proposal to be agreed upon and presented to the FIA's World Motor Sport Council in Shanghai next month.

Alpine team boss Flavio Briatore said the agreement for 2030 was all but signed.

"We have the agreement, basically. It's not signed, but it looks like everybody's agreed to 2030 V8s, and I'm very happy," Briatore said. "I think it's the right way to go.

"We need an engine with a lot of noise, and a simple engine, and we need to be racing with that because, in the end, I believe the best for the spectator, for everybody is a very simple engine, a lot of noise and basta.

"Maybe have some KERS [Kinetic Energy Recovery Systems] or stuff like that, nothing major like we have now."

The current regulations, which require nearly 50% of peak power to come from the power unit's battery, were introduced to keep the sport road-car relevant and entice more engine manufacturers to F1.

In that sense they were successful, with Audi joining this season, Honda returning from the brink of leaving the sport to team up with Aston Martin, and Ford partnering with Red Bull's in-house powertrains department.

However, the emphasis on electric power has proved controversial this year, with drivers forced to change their driving style to manage energy around a lap instead of pushing the cars to the limit.

Two-time champion Fernando Alonso labelled this year's regulations a "battery world championship" following the second race of the season in China, with the sport later agreeing to tweak certain rules to limit the unusual behaviour of the hybrid systems by the fourth round in Miami.

Further changes are planned over the next two seasons to shift the 50/50 split between electrical power and internal combustion engine (ICE) power to 60/40 in favour of the ICE by 2028.

V8 engines were last used in F1 in 2013 and featured a mild hybrid boost known as the Kinetic Energy Recovery System.

The previous era of V8s were known for their evocative exhaust note, but the turbocharged versions proposed for 2030 are not expected to be as loud or high-pitched due to the presence of a turbocharger.

stories.headline: 2027 WNBA mock draft: Tempo win lottery, projected to pick JuJu Watkins at No. 1
stories.summary: Toronto edged Houston and got the top pick in Sunday's draft lottery. The Comets will pick No. 2 and the Mystics No. 3.
stories.body:
In what could be the JuJu Watkins sweepstakes, the Toronto Tempo will have the No. 1 pick in the 2027 WNBA draft. The Tempo won the draft lottery Sunday, with the Houston Comets picking second and the Washington Mystics third.

The Seattle Storm have the No. 4 pick, the Portland Fire got No. 5 and the Los Angeles Sparks have Nos. 6 and 7.

The Tempo, an expansion team in 2026, finished 11-33 last season, missing the playoffs. They were last in the league in defensive rating and won just one game after the All-Star break.

All of that could be much improved in 2027 with a player such as Watkins in Toronto. The national player of the year as a sophomore for the USC Trojans, Watkins missed last season after a knee injury suffered in the 2025 NCAA tournament. She has looked great so far this season and would fit in well with any WNBA team.

This is just Watkins' third college season, but age-wise, she is eligible for the draft. It is unknown if she will go pro or return to USC, but for now we are including her in the mock draft. If she decides Toronto is an unappealing destination or just wants to spend another season in college, she can wait until the 2028 draft.

That said, there is also uncertainty about the seniors who already have completed three seasons. Under the NCAA's new age-based eligibility model -- the five-seasons-in-five-years rule -- they could return for the 2027-28 season. So a lot about the draft pool remains speculative.

But now we know the lottery order.

1. Toronto Tempo: JuJu Watkins
USC | guard | 6-foot-2 | senior

Watkins and the Trojans are 3-1 after a close loss Sunday to No. 1 South Carolina in which she had 25 points. The March 2025 knee injury that forced Watkins to miss last season has not slowed her. She is averaging 24.5 points, 6.8 rebounds, 3.5 assists and 3.3 steals. The Tempo's strength last season was at guard, led by Marina Mabrey. If Watkins doesn't declare for the draft, there should still be good players available for the Tempo. But perhaps not an immediate franchise-changer as Watkins is expected to be.

2. Houston Comets: Madison Booker
Texas | forward | 6-foot-1 | senior

Like several teams, Texas has not been tested yet. But Booker has displayed why she's a lottery pick in the three games she has played so far, including a 30-point, six-assist game against Northern Colorado. Booker's size, strength and confidence on offense and her versatility on defense should translate to the pro game. She took a hard fall in Wednesday's win over South Dakota State and did not play in Sunday's victory against Tarleton State, but she is not expected to miss much more time. The Comets -- the Connecticut Sun relocated as a revived franchise -- last played in the 2008 WNBA season. The Sun were tied for next to last with Toronto at 11-33 this year, and it's fair to say they could use help in all areas, which would make Booker appealing.

3. Washington Mystics: Hannah Hidalgo
Notre Dame | guard | 5-foot-6 | senior

Hidalgo has carried a heavy load throughout her college career, and that continues her senior season. In four victories, she has averaged 28.3 points, 7.5 rebounds, 5.5 assists and 4.8 steals while shooting 59.4% from the field. Hidalgo is a huge threat on offense and defense and could really add to the young core already there if she goes to the Mystics. Washington could use more 3-point shooting. While Hidalgo wasn't great from beyond the arc last season (36 of 142, 25.4%), she shot 40% from 3-point range as a sophomore and is at 40% so far this season.

4. Seattle Storm: Tessa Johnson
South Carolina | guard | 6-foot-1 | senior

Johnson's 3-point shooting is an impressive tool that will translate to the pro game. She was the top power-conference player in the country last season in 3-point percentage (44.8%, 90 of 201). So far this season, she is 9-for-18 (50%) from beyond the arc and is averaging 17.0 points. She had 28 points in Sunday's victory over USC. The Storm were last in the WNBA this past season at 8-36 and could benefit from another dynamic young guard to go along with the young post talent they have.

5. Portland Fire: Mikaylah Williams
LSU | guard | 6-foot | senior

The Tigers have cruised through four blowouts, and Williams' averages -- 19.0 points, 5.3 rebounds and 5.5 assists while shooting 58% from the field and 45.5% from beyond the arc -- don't tell us anything we didn't expect. She's a pro-ready player on the offensive end who can look to improve defensively in the WNBA. The expansion Fire had a solid season in 2025, going 17-27, and Williams could fit in offensively.

6. Los Angeles Sparks: Kymora Johnson
Virginia | guard | 5-foot-7 | senior

The Cavaliers are 5-0, and we will know more about them once they play their tougher nonconference foes, such as Oklahoma on Nov. 23. But so far, Johnson has looked very good, averaging 18.8 points, 5.2 rebounds, 5.4 assists and 2.2 steals while shooting 59.6% from the field and 61.3% from beyond the arc (13 of 21). With back-to-back picks, Los Angeles can address two of several needs with this draft. The Sparks were 16-28 this season and missed the playoffs for the sixth year in a row.

7. Los Angeles Sparks: Sarah Cissé
France | forward | 6-foot-2

There's so much we don't know now about the Sparks -- including who their coach will be for 2027 -- as they move on after future Hall of Famer Nneka Ogwumike's retirement. But Cissé is another talented player out of France who could make an impact on the WNBA. The MVP of the U20 European Championships this summer, she turns 20 in January. The Sparks were next to last in the WNBA in rebounding this past season, so Cissé might be able to help there.

8. New York Liberty: Ainhoa Risacher
France | forward | 6-foot-1

If you recognize the last name, Risacher is the younger sister of Zaccharie Risacher, the NBA's No. 1 draft pick in 2024. A good-sized wing player, Risacher competed alongside Cissé on France's winning U20 European Championships team this past summer. She will turn 20 in July. The Liberty had an up-and-down 2026 season, getting the No. 8 seed in the playoffs. They knocked off No. 1 Minnesota but then were swept by No. 4 Atlanta. New York fired Chris DeMarco after just one season, so we await their next coach. The Liberty already have a strong French/international presence. The question might be if Risacher impresses them enough defensively compared with other draft options.

9. Dallas Wings: Chloe Kitts
South Carolina | forward | 6-foot-2 | senior

Kitts missed last season because of a knee injury but has looked great so far. A starter as a junior, she averaged 10.2 points and 7.7 rebounds in 2024-25. Through four games this season, she has three double-doubles and is averaging 13.0 points and 10.0 rebounds. In Sunday's victory over USC, Kitts had 15 points, 12 rebounds, three assists and four steals. If she continues to play this well, we could see her move up the draft board. Still, with Dallas having young guards such as Paige Bueckers and Azzi Fudd, Kitts could be a good addition for the Wings, who made the playoffs at 27-17 this season.

10. Indiana Fever: Talaysia Cooper
Ole Miss | guard | 6-foot-0 | senior

The Fever are facing two huge offseason questions: Will free agent guard Kelsey Mitchell return, and who will be their general manager? Indiana could use help at the wing position with a player who can defend at a high level but also score. That could be Cooper, who is playing for her third SEC program and averaging 14.0 points while shooting 37% (10 of 27) from 3-point range. She showed progress from beyond the arc last season, and if that continues this season it will help her draft prospects. Cooper had her best defensive season as a sophomore at Tennessee, and a return to that level will boost her.

11. Chicago Sky: Khamil Pierre
NC State | forward | 6-foot-2 | senior

Pierre doesn't shoot the 3 much, but she is relentless in the paint. After two strong years at Vanderbilt, she transferred to NC State and led the ACC in rebounding last season (11.9 RPG) while averaging 16.7 points and shooting 52.5% from the field. So far this season for the 4-1 Wolfpack, she is averaging 21.2 points and 8.4 rebounds while shooting 51.3%. The injury-plagued Sky went 16-28 and missed the playoffs for the third year in a row this past season. They were 13th in offensive rating and 10th in rebounding, and Pierre might help in both areas.

12. Chicago Sky: S'Mya Nichols
Kansas | guard | 6-foot | senior

Nichols is off to a little slower start than expected, averaging 12.5 points and 4.3 assists. (She averaged 17.4 and 4.6 last season.) That's why she has fallen from No. 6 in our two previous mock drafts. But to be fair, it's still early in the season. Nichols had 12 points and six assists in the Jayhawks' loss to Nebraska on Saturday. She and Kansas have another shot at a ranked team this week at Minnesota on Wednesday.

13. Dallas Wings: Kaylene Smikle
Tennessee | guard | 6-foot-0 | senior

Smikle started her career at Rutgers, then went to Maryland and is now at Tennessee. She played just seven games last year with the Terps, missing the rest of the season after knee surgery. So far this season, she is leading the 4-0 Lady Vols with 22.3 points per game, while also averaging 6.0 rebounds. She is also off to a hot start from beyond the arc at 50% (12 of 24). Smikle could add guard/wing depth for Dallas.

14. Golden State Valkyries: Oluchi Okananwa
Maryland | guard | 5-foot-10 | senior

Okananwa is averaging 14.0 points and 6.3 rebounds, but the Terps have played just three games. She was first-team All-Big Ten and all-defense last season -- we know the WNBA champion Valkyries love defense -- but she probably will need to show improvement as a 3-point shooter to ensure being a first-round pick. So far this season she is 3-for-6 from beyond the arc.

15. Minnesota Lynx: Clara Strack
Kentucky | center | 6-foot-5 | senior

Sunday was another big stats day for Strack, who had 29 points and 18 rebounds in a victory over Eastern Michigan. That included going 4-of-5 from beyond the arc, which is important: It's not easy for traditional centers to find their way in the WNBA, so having shooting range matters. Strack has shown that, making 42 3-pointers over the past two seasons. She is 8-of-21 from 3-point range so far this season. Strack, who was the SEC's defensive player of the year in 2025, is averaging 18.4 points, 9.6 rebounds and 3.8 blocks for the 5-0 Wildcats.

stories.headline: Abu Dhabi court reduces sentences for 8 in Nurmagomedov-Dvalishvili brawl
stories.summary: An Abu Dhabi court has reduced the sentences of eight defendants, including six members of Team Nurmagomedov, for their part in last week's wild hotel brawl in the UAE's capital city.
stories.body:
Abu Dhabi's Criminal Court has reduced the sentences of eight defendants convicted in connection to last week's hotel brawl involving Usman Nurmagomedov and Merab Dvalishvili, according to the Abu Dhabi Judicial Department.

The eight defendants, including six members of Team Nurmagomedov, were originally sentenced to six months in prison. Under the revised ruling, which the ADJD released Tuesday, each defendant will instead pay a fine of 150,000 AED (approximately $40,800). The department said the reduced sentence followed a reconciliation between the parties, the mutual withdrawal of claims and appeal by the victim to the Abu Dhabi government for their release.

The altercation took place Nov. 11 in the lobby of the Yas Hilton Hotel, ahead of RAF's inaugural event in Abu Dhabi. Multiple videos captured Nurmagomedov, who is the PFL lightweight champion and younger cousin of Khabib Nurmagomedov, approach Dvalishvili from behind and slap him in the face, triggering a brawl between multiple members of both teams. Dvalishvili, who was initially arrested but released, advocated for Nurmagomedov's release Saturday.

Nurmagomedov and Dvalishvili have been involved in a long-running feud, dating back to Dvalishvili's UFC title win against Umar Nurmagomedov, Usman's older brother, in January 2025. The camps were involved in a brief altercation at another RAF event in July in Dvalishvili's home country of Georgia. Over the weekend, UFC president Dana White criticized RAF's security measures, saying, "They must like it for this to happen all the time."

RAF founder Chad Bronstein told ESPN the organization regretted the incident, but pushed back on any suggestion it's becoming commonplace.

"Did they have drama in the past? Yeah," Bronstein said of Nurmagomedov and Dvalishvili. "But did I think that was going to happen in Abu Dhabi? No. You can always expect there's going to be some words in a press conference ... I didn't think that would happen in a hotel lobby. How many fights have taken place at the UFC, at press conferences, in arenas? We have a great relationship with the UFC, but I think that's an unfair statement."

Bronstein added the incident did not impact RAF's recently-signed deal with the region of Abu Dhabi.

"We're already talking about new events coming up, we have a five-year deal," Bronstein said. "Saturday's event sold out Etihad Arena. I feel like there's going to be a long partnership."

On Monday, RAF announced Dvalishvili and his 21-year-old Georgian teammate Saba Lazishvili have been booked to the promotion's first event in the New York metropolitan area on Dec. 19 at Nassau Coliseum in Long Island.

Dvalishvili will face Kenzo Biyong, a former Dutch professional soccer player from the Netherlands. Lazashvili, who gained a massive online following for his participation in the hotel lobby brawl, will face the winner of a match between Sergio Garcia and Cody Garbrandt at RAF 15 on Nov. 28 in Chicago.

stories.headline: First-half romp powers Jillaroos' fourth-straight Rugby League World Cup salute
stories.summary: Australia's Jillaroos have blown away New Zealand 34-10 to win a fourth-straight Women's Rugby League World Cup.
stories.body:
Australia have underlined their women's rugby league dominance with a 34-10 annihilation of New Zealand in the World Cup final.

The Jillaroos did the damage with six first-half tries on Sunday at Suncorp Stadium, with winger Jaime Chapman recording a brilliant hat-trick before the break to cap a historic tournament.

It was Australia's fourth straight Cup triumph, following a 54-4 win in the final four years ago and coming after New Zealand won the first three tournaments between 2000-08.

Chapman carried two players more than 10 metres to score her first, before flying into the corner for another and then busting through four tacklers for a sensational 70-metre solo effort.

Her treble gave her the equal record for tries in a World Cup -- for men or women -- at 13, matching the Kiwi Ferns' Honey Hireme-Smiler from 2017.

It seemed inevitable that she would go clear in the second half.

But both teams struggled in the Brisbane humidity, with the Kiwi Ferns' try in the finals seconds the only points of an error-riddled second period.

For the Jillaroos there were several poignant narratives to come out of the win.

Coach Jess Skinner's controversial decision to play five-eighth Jesse Southwell and drop Jocelyn Kelleher paid dividends.

Southwell schemed with the ball, landed five goals and was the perfect foil for half Tarryn Aiken, who controlled play with confidence and skill.

Chapman played in the pool games and semi-final in the 2022 World Cup but has now put an indelible stamp on a final.

"There is no better win than winning the World Cup on home turf," she told Channel Seven.

"We connected the first day we came into camp."

Fullback Tamika Upton sat out the tournament four years ago with a calf injury but now the five-time premiership winner has every team accolade in the game to her credit.

Prop Millie Elliott retires with a fairytale ending while dual international Sariah Paki, who was chased by the Ferns to play for them, has now won the World Cup in two sports after triumphing with the Australian rugby sevens side in 2022.

All the talk before the clash was the danger posed by New Zealand's Golden Boot winner and strike centre Stacey Waaka.

The former rugby union star, who had scored nine tries in the tournament, was snuffed out by Jillaroos captain Isabelle Kelly, who confronted Waaka all match and gave her no space.

As the Jillaroos' big guns stood up, centre Jessica Sergis scored her 23rd try in 18 Tests with a 70m dash through the middle off an undetected forward pass.

Aiken turned second-rower Shaylee Bent inside for the second try of the match while Upton started and finished a movement that had her attacking fingerprints all over it.

Ferns fullback Apii Nicholls was her side's best player in a dynamic display until she tore a hamstring in the 66th minute.
